I sit here, empty screen. The cursor blinks. The task is simple: write whatever comes. But the mind resists, scrambling for something meaningful. Yet meaning isn't required. Only words.

I think about the word "whatever." It is a shrugging word, a dismissive word. Also an invitation. Whatever comes. Like opening a tap. The water may be cloudy at first. Let it run.

Outside, the rain. It comes in sheaves, whispers. I imagine each drop a letter, falling from a gray sky onto the pavement. The street is a page. The water writes its own text, then vanishes. All writing is like that: a temporary carving against forgetfulness. But perhaps forgetfulness is the real canvas.

Memory is the thing I keep returning to. Why? Maybe because it's the only place I can truly go without a ticket. The past is my private country. I can re-enter it through any doorway—a scent, a song, a particular slant of light in late afternoon. Just now, the smell of rain on warm asphalt brought me to a summer in my childhood. I was small, barefoot, catching toads in the backyard. The world was huge then. The grass was a jungle. The sky was a sea. My grandmother called from the porch, her voice floating across the lawn like a bird. "Come in! It's going to rain!" But I stayed. I stayed until the first cool drops fell on my shoulders, until the soil darkened, until I felt the drumming on the roof of my skull. That was joy, raw and uncomplicated.

Now joy is complicated. It has layers, conditions, fears attached. Maybe that's what growing up means: the gradual accretion of consequences. Every act weighed, every word considered. We trade the immediacy of the toad-catching self for the cautious, planning self. Yet sometimes, in a dream or a fever, the old self surfaces, hungry and alive.

I wonder if words are my toads now. I catch them, hold them gently, let them go. Some are slimy, some leap. Some are imaginary. What is a writer but a collector of slippery things? We spend our lives chasing syntax, hoping to pin down a feeling before it disappears. But the feeling always escapes. The description is not the thing. Yet the description is all we have.

Let me change course. Let me talk about clouds. Clouds are like thoughts: they form, they drift, they dissolve. No two alike. Each one a temporary arrangement of water and air. If I lie on the grass and watch them, I can almost see a horse, a whale, a sleeping giant. It is the oldest form of storytelling—patterning the sky. Our ancestors did it too, seeing gods in thunderheads, omens in cirrus. The sky was the first screen, and humanity has never stopped projecting.

There is a kind of peace in watching clouds. It teaches a quiet acceptance of transience. Here now, gone in minutes. Nothing is lost, because nothing is possessed. Maybe that's the secret at the heart of all spiritual practice: to watch your own mind the way you watch clouds. Let the thoughts come, let them go, don't clutch at the pretty ones, don't scream at the dark ones. Just witness. But I am not good at witnessing. I want to hold, to write down, to make permanent. It's the curse of my kind.

What else? Food. Memory of bread baking. The smell of yeast and warmth, the hollow sound when you knock on a loaf. My mother's hands, flour-dusted, folding dough. She would give me a pinch of the raw dough to bite—a sweet, slippery mass that tasted of the future. Later, eating the baked bread, I would think of that raw moment, how the future is always raw until it is baked. Now when I bake bread myself, I feel her presence in the kitchen. I use her movements, remember her patience. The bread they bake in heaven, someone once wrote, is the bread our mothers made. I am not religious, but this feels true.

Love. I should talk about love. But what can be said that hasn't been said? Love is the strange gravity that pulls two strangers into orbit. The precision of its timing—how you meet the person you would have missed entirely if you'd been thirty seconds later. It's all luck. All terrifying luck. And yet we build cathedrals around that luck, give it vows, children, whole lives. We take the random and make it sacred. That is love's miracle: not that it exists, but that we choose to believe in its significance. We write poems, we buy rings, we build a temple around a coincidence.

Love is also the ordinary. The unglamorous daily mercy of two people doing dishes, arguing about the thermostat, holding hands in a hospital. The romance of constancy. I think of my grandparents, celebrating sixty years together. My grandfather had a habit of squeezing my grandmother's hand three times—a secret code meaning "I love you." She told me once: "When he forgets to do it, I know something is wrong." It is the smallest wordless gesture, and it contains an entire marriage. I want to write a story about that. Maybe I will. A story about three squeezes, about the life contained in a single gesture.

But the cursor blinks. The rain has stopped. The white screen remains. This is the writer's true task: to sit with the blankness without panicking. To trust that something will come. Something always does. It may not be brilliant; it may be clouds or toads or bread or three squeezes. It may be a wandering, formless reflection of a mind trying to understand itself. But it is the work of being human: to take the fleeting and give it shape.

"Whatever comes to you"—it's a wise instruction. It asks for surrender. Not to the world, but to the mind's own river. And so I have written about rain and memory and clouds and bread and love. Perhaps it's a letter to myself, a map of the territory I carry. The words are poured onto the page like water. They are a small architecture against silence. They are my hand reaching out, three squeezes, a code for "I was here."

There are exactly—well, not exactly—but there are enough words now. The screen, once empty, is full. The cursor still blinks, but it is less anxious. The rain is gone, but the streets remember. Everything is remembered, somewhere. I am still searching for myself, word by word. And maybe that is the whole secret: we are not the ones writing. The writing is writing us. We just sit down, open the tap, and let the whatever pour through.

I close my eyes and hear the rain again. It is always raining somewhere. The words are always coming. I only need to meet them halfway. This is what I have to offer: a handful of thoughts, a trail of letters. Take them as they are. Damp, alive, fading. Like footprints on the pavement, telling you someone passed this way. And then the sky clears, and the sun comes out, and the whole world shines, wet and new, ready for a different story.
